Which of the following could represent the level curves of the surface $z=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ shown above?
worked_solution:
First, notice that the range of $f(x,y)$ is $[-1,1].$ So, we will consider only $c$-level curves for $c\in [-1,1].$

The level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equations 

$$
f(x,y)=c
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =c \\ x & =\pm \operatorname{arccos}⁡c+2\pi n\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ can be any integer. 

Notice that in the equations $x=\pm \operatorname{arccos}⁡c+2\pi n$ do not depend on $y.$ So, for a given $c\in [-1,1]$ and integer $n$, the right-hand side of the equation is constant. As a result, we obtain a family of vertical lines, as shown below.

We notice the following:

- Each vector in our vector field is parallel to the $y$-axis. So, the $i$ and $k$ components of our vector field are zero everywhere. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
H(x,y,z)=i+k
$$

- Moreover, each vector in our vector field is pointing in the *positive* $y$-direction, so the $j$ component of our vector field is positive. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
F(x,y,z)=-2\,j
$$

- Finally, we note that each vector in our vector field has the same length, so the $j$ component of our vector field is constant. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
K(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $G(x,y,z)=3\,j.$
